questions.q: What does `kubectl set image deployment/web-app web-app=...:1.4.3` actually trigger?
options: It deletes the Deployment and requires `kubectl apply` to recreate it from scratch
It edits every running Pod's container in place without creating any new objects
The Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet with the updated Pod template and begins shifting replicas to it
It only updates the image tag shown in `kubectl describe`, with no effect on running Pods
questions.explain: Updating a Deployment's image is exactly the mechanism from Lesson 10: the Deployment creates a brand-new ReplicaSet reflecting the new template and gradually shifts replicas from the old ReplicaSet to the new one.

questions.q: In a rolling update strategy with `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge: 1` on a Deployment with `replicas: 3`, what does `maxUnavailable: 0` guarantee?
options: The rollout can never drop below 3 available Pods — a new Pod must be ready before an old one is removed
The Deployment is temporarily allowed to run with zero healthy Pods during the swap
No more than 1 Pod total can exist until the rollout finishes
Pods from the old ReplicaSet are deleted before any new Pod is created
questions.explain: maxUnavailable: 0 means capacity can never dip below the target replica count during the rollout; a new Pod must come up fully before an old one is removed. maxSurge: 1 is what permits briefly going one Pod above target to make that possible.

questions.q: Why can `kubectl rollout status` be used as a health gate inside a CI/CD pipeline step?
options: It only prints log lines and never affects the pipeline's exit code
It blocks until the rollout finishes or fails, returning a non-zero exit code if new Pods never become ready, instead of hanging silently
It automatically rolls back any failed deployment on its own
It is the only command that can trigger a rolling update at all
questions.explain: kubectl rollout status blocks and reports success or failure explicitly, which is exactly the signal a pipeline step needs to decide whether a deploy succeeded.

questions.q: What mechanism makes a Deployment rollback possible at all, without re-applying an old manifest file?
options: Kubernetes keeps scaled-down previous ReplicaSets around as revision history, and rollback scales a prior one back up while scaling the current one down
etcd stores a separate full backup of every Deployment automatically every hour
kubectl caches every previous manifest locally and resubmits it on undo
Rollback is only possible if `--record` was passed on the original apply command
questions.explain: Kubernetes doesn't delete old ReplicaSets on update — it scales them to zero and retains them as revisions. kubectl rollout undo reverses the exact same mechanism a forward rollout uses, just scaling the old ReplicaSet back up.

questions.q: What does `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web-app --to-revision=1` do differently from a plain `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web-app`?
options: It performs an instant, non-gradual switch instead of a rolling update
It deletes all revision history after rolling back
It requires the Deployment to be scaled to zero first
It reverts to a specific named revision rather than just the immediately prior one
questions.explain: Plain rollout undo reverts to the immediately prior revision. Adding --to-revision lets you target any specific retained revision from kubectl rollout history instead.
